idiom_name: shared state in the companion object, instance methods delegate to it
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no static members; class-level state lives in the companion object, a single object bound to the class and initialized when the class is resolved, so putting the shared variables there and letting instance methods read and write them reproduces the monostate exactly (members are reached through the class name, and @JvmStatic only affects Java interop). What replaces the classic structure is the companion object itself - the language's documented replacement for static members - and because it is an object it can implement interfaces and be passed around, which makes test seams easier to add than with Java statics. Keep the state private to the companion and expose behaviour from the class; prefer an ordinary instance passed to the constructor whenever the sharing is not intrinsic to the concept.
pitfalls: The companion object is initialized when the class is loaded (the semantics of a Java static initializer), so a state initializer that depends on another class's companion can run before its dependency is ready.
Companion members are one per class and reachable from anywhere through the class name, so the shared state is a global by another name; keep it private and expose behaviour rather than the variable.
A companion object is not inherited: every subclass shares the same companion and therefore the same state, and there is no per-subclass copy unless the subclass declares its own.
